cards.title: Fu Wen (付稳)
cards.sub: 2017 · technical lead, Weibo hybrid-cloud DCP project
cards.prompt: Weibo's hybrid-cloud lead sorted the platform's peaks into two classes. Name both, and give the single number DCP was built to hit.
cards.body: Not a feed designer — a capacity engineer. He split Weibo's peaks into the Spring Festival gala, whose date is known a year ahead, and celebrity hot events such as a couple going public, which he described as abrupt and unforecastable. DCP's goal was stated as one capability: finish scaling 1,000 nodes inside ten minutes.
cards.answer: The annual Spring Festival peak, which sits on the calendar and can be provisioned months ahead, and celebrity hot events, which arrive with no warning at all. DCP's target was 1,000 nodes scaled out within ten minutes.

cards.title: Lu Han introduces his girlfriend
cards.prompt: One sentence posted at noon on a Sunday took Weibo out. Who posted it, what did it say, and how long was the platform unusable?
cards.body: Lu Han introduced the actress Guan Xiaotong in one line, translated: "Hi everyone, I want to introduce my girlfriend @GuanXiaoTong to you." So many fans commented that the platform was inaccessible for two hours. Not a bad deploy, not a lost datacentre: one account, one sentence, one afternoon.
cards.answer: Lu Han, on 8 October 2017, in translation: "Hi everyone, I want to introduce my girlfriend @GuanXiaoTong to you." The volume of fan comments left Weibo inaccessible for two hours; SCMP reports full server function returned around 4pm.

cards.title: "Follow Whom? Chinese Users Have Different Choice"
cards.sub: Chen, Liu, Wang & Gu · arXiv:1212.0167 · December 2012
cards.prompt: Which open measurement of Weibo's follow graph can you read today, how big was the crawl, and what did it find that stops you copying a US fanout threshold?
cards.body: An arXiv paper (cs.SI) built on 80.8 million Sina Weibo profiles and 7.2 billion follow relations, compared against a Twitter dataset. Its finding: Weibo's following preference is more concentrated and hierarchical than Twitter's — people follow upward. So the tail you size fanout for is not Twitter's tail.
cards.answer: Chen, Liu, Wang and Gu, arXiv:1212.0167, December 2012 — 80.8 million profiles and 7.2 billion relations. Weibo's following preference is more concentrated and hierarchical than Twitter's, so the shape of the tail, and therefore the push/pull threshold, does not transfer.

cards.title: DCP, the ten-minute fleet
cards.sub: 2016 Spring Festival · Weibo with Alibaba Cloud
cards.prompt: Weibo answered an unforecastable write burst by renting a second fleet. What did that fleet deliver at the 2016 Spring Festival, and why is rented capacity still not an answer to fanout?
cards.body: Weibo and Alibaba Cloud deployed public-cloud capacity only hours before the peak: more than 1,000 ECS instances created dynamically, carrying 60% of core traffic, average scale-out under ten minutes. Rented capacity shortens the queue. It does not shorten anybody's follower list.
cards.answer: More than 1,000 Alibaba Cloud ECS instances, created dynamically, taking 60% of core traffic, with an average scale-out under ten minutes. It buys throughput, not fewer writes — one post is still one write per follower, so where you cut the fanout is still the load-bearing decision.
